Facebook Twitter Print Email COP31: Cities rise up the climate agenda as leaders face demands for action Conference coverage By Laura Quinones in Antalya 12 November 2026 Climate and Environment From flooded homes to melting Himalayan glaciers, the human cost of climate change took centre stage at COP31 on Thursday, as world leaders turned their attention to protecting cities and vulnerable communities, while activists challenged governments to do more. Today at COP31 Resilient cities: Leaders hold a historic dialogue on housing, urban resilience and climate action. Leaders’ Summit: Vulnerable countries demand greater protection and access to climate finance. Negotiations: Divisions persist over funding adaptation and accelerating climate action. Climate justice: Greta Thunberg joins activists from Nepal and Australia in demanding change. Disaster risk financing : New UN platform aims to unlock more than $3 billion to protect 75 million people from climate shocks by 2030. Climate change is often paired with images of melting glaciers, disappearing forests and devastating fires. But for millions living in cities, the crisis is increasingly knocking on their doors. The signs are everywhere: in floodwaters pouring into family homes, unbearable heat inside poorly built housing, and neighbourhoods where inadequate drainage turns heavy rains into disaster. “Perhaps we have to change … the imaginary when we talk and think about climate change,” UN-Habitat Executive Director Anacláudia Rossbach told UN News on the sidelines of COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye. Her message was simple: cities are on the front lines of climate change, and protecting them means protecting the people who live there. UNU-EHS/Austin Gonzales Anacláudia Rossbach, head of UN-Habitat. A historic moment for cities For the first time at a UN climate conference, the COP31 Leaders' Summit dedicated a high-level dialogue to urban resilience, adaptation and climate action. The meeting brought together national and local leaders, financial institutions and other partners to address a growing challenge: up to three billion people lack adequate housing, while more than one billion live in informal settlements, often exposed to floods, landslides and extreme heat. In remarks delivered on behalf of Secretary-General António Guterres , UN-Habitat chief Anacláudia Rossbach stressed that housing must be at the heart of climate action. “Housing is climate action. Urban planning is climate action. Access to basic services is climate action,” she said. Tweet URL Speaking separately to UN News , she called for greater attention to the poorest communities, particularly those living in informal settlements, who have fewer resources to prepare for disasters or recover from them. Protecting them requires more than stronger buildings. It also means access to drainage, sanitation, electricity and water, backed by better urban planning and financing. “We need systemic change,” Ms. Rossbach said, underscoring the importance of partnerships among governments, banks, businesses and communities. There are signs of progress. A new UN-Habitat analysis found that 80 per cent of national climate plans now contain well-developed urban measures, up from 50 per cent in the previous round. Yet cities need around $4.5 trillion in climate investment annually through 2030, while current financing covers only about one-fifth of that amount. For Ms. Rossbach, the meeting marked a turning point. “We brought everybody that we need to bring together at this meeting,” she said, expressing hope that cities would gain a stronger voice in future negotiations and better access to financing. Mayors step up In other positive news, 69 mayors representing more than 250 million people committed to another year of climate action through the Yearly Offer of Action initiative, a 60 per cent increase from last year. Their plans include flood-warning systems in Addis Ababa, London's first dedicated heat plan and incentives to improve the environmental performance of 400 commercial buildings in Melbourne. World leaders confront the cost of climate disasters At the second day of the Leaders’ Summit , developing nations renewed appeals for support as they grapple with mounting climate-related losses.
